question: My baby has a temperature of 100.4F. What should I do?
what_to_check: Under 3 months: call the pediatrician right away
answer: A temperature of 100.4°F (38°C) or higher in a baby requires you to call your pediatrician immediately. Do not wait to see if other symptoms develop — contact your doctor right away, even if your baby seems otherwise fine.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your pediatrician immediately if your baby has a temperature of 100.4°F (38°C) or higher. For babies 3–6 months, call if the fever reaches 101°F (38.3°C) or greater. For babies older than 6 months, call if the temperature is 103°F (39.4°C) or higher. Also be aware that a raised body temperature from heatstroke is a separate dangerous condition requiring 911.

question: Can a fever cause a seizure?
what_to_check: Febrile seizures, roughly 6 months to 5 years
answer: Yes, fever can cause seizures in young children. These are called febrile seizures or febrile convulsions. During a febrile seizure, a child may get an odd look on their face, then stiffen or twitch, roll their eyes, and be unresponsive for a short time. Their skin may also appear darker than usual. The good news is that febrile seizures are almost always harmless and typically last less than one minute, causing no lasting damage to the brain or nervous system.
when_to_call_doctor: You should tell your pediatrician promptly if your child has ANY febrile seizure. Call 911 immediately if your child is having trouble breathing OR if the febrile seizure does not stop within 15 minutes. A very high temperature may also point to a significant infection or dehydration that needs treatment.

question: Why does my child get a fever in the first place?
what_to_check: Part of the immune response (white blood cells fighting infection)
answer: Your child gets a fever because their body is fighting off an infection. The body activates its immune defenses, such as white blood cells, which attack and destroy invading bacteria and viruses. The fever is essentially the body's natural response to these invaders. It is important to figure out the cause of the fever so it can be properly treated.

what_to_check: Roseola: rash starts 12 to 24 hours after the fever ends
answer: Based on the symptoms you're describing — a rash appearing after the fever goes away — this sounds like it could be Roseola. Roseola is a common viral illness where a child has 3 to 5 days of high fever with no rash, and then the rash appears 12 to 24 hours after the fever goes away. The rash looks like pink, small, flat spots that start on the chest and stomach and then spread to the face. It typically lasts 1 to 3 days. Most viral rashes go away within 48 hours.

question: Can a medicine cause a rash?
what_to_check: Drug rashes cannot be diagnosed over the phone
answer: Yes, medicines can sometimes cause rashes. Prescription medicines sometimes cause widespread rashes, though most are not allergic reactions. Non-prescription (OTC) medicines rarely cause rashes. Interestingly, when a rash appears while a child is taking a fever medicine like acetaminophen or ibuprofen, it is most often a viral rash — not caused by the medicine itself. This is because most viral rashes start with a fever, and the child is already taking fever medicine when the rash appears. If your child is taking an antibiotic and develops a rash, only about 10% of those cases turn out to be true allergic drug rashes — the rest are viral rashes.
when_to_call_doctor: Any widespread rash accompanied by fever needs to be seen by a doctor, as some serious infections can cause this type of rash. Do not try to diagnose it at home.
